Editor's note: Campbell Brown anchors CNN's "Campbell Brown: No Bias, No Bull" at 8 p.m. ET Mondays through Fridays. She delivered this commentary during the "Cutting through the Bull" segment of Monday night's broadcast. CNN's Campbell Brown says nonemergency legislation needs time to be read by the public and Congress. (CNN) -- Whether by omission or commission, both the White House and Congress get a dose of blame for not living up to the new era of transparency promised by President Obama. The president's old campaign Web site still has this commitment there for all to see: . "As president, Obama will not sign any nonemergency bill without giving the American public an opportunity to review and comment on the White House Web site for five days." Well, the president broke that promise barely a week after taking office when he signed the Lilly Ledbetter Bill dealing with equal pay for men and women. A good bill, and certainly one that could have survived a five-day comment period. So, maybe the White House folks just forgot? But then there is Congress and the Stimulus Bill. How fast could you get through it? According to the nonpartisan Sunlight Foundation, lawmakers had just 13 hours to read 1,100 pages of material that would cost the American taxpayer $787 billion. That's less than a minute and a half per page, with no time for bathroom breaks. No wonder so many of our lawmakers didn't seem to notice that last-minute exemption clearing the way for bailed-out companies like AIG to pay out big bonuses. So, the House tried to clean up the mess last week by rushing through another bill -- a tax on AIG bonuses. That bill was just 11 hours old before it went on the floor to be argued and then quickly approved. And the list goes on well before the president took office. The bank bailout got all of 29 hours, the rescue of Fannie and Freddie was only available for 19 hours. This is how bills could literally become, to borrow a phrase, too big to fail -- and too fast to stop. The Sunlight Foundation is calling on Congress to allow the American people three days, 72 hours, to read a nonemergency bill online before debate begins. We strongly agree. And yes lawmakers, you can have three days to read it over, too, before taking a stand. As for President Obama's promise of a five-day public review once a bill leaves Capitol Hill headed for his desk, it would be nice if he kept his word on this going forward. The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of Campbell Brown.

**Editor's Note:** Campbell Brown anchors CNN's "Campbell Brown: No Bias, No Bull" at 8 p.m. ET, Monday through Friday. She delivered this commentary during the "Cutting through the Bull" segment of Monday night's broadcast. CNN's Campbell Brown argues that nonemergency legislation requires sufficient time to be reviewed by both the public and Congress.

**(CNN)** -- Whether through omission or commission, both the White House and Congress deserve their share of blame for failing to uphold the new era of transparency promised by President Obama.

The president's former campaign website still displays this commitment for all to see: "As president, Obama will not sign any nonemergency bill without giving the American public an opportunity to review and comment on the White House website for five days."

Yet the president broke that promise barely a week after taking office, when he signed the Lilly Ledbetter Bill addressing equal pay for men and women. It was a worthy piece of legislation—and certainly one that could have withstood a five-day comment period. So perhaps the White House staff simply forgot?

Then there is Congress and the Stimulus Bill. How quickly could you possibly read through it? According to the nonpartisan Sunlight Foundation, lawmakers had a mere 13 hours to examine 1,100 pages of material carrying a price tag of $787 billion for American taxpayers. That amounts to less than a minute and a half per page—with no time even for a bathroom break.

Little wonder, then, that so many of our lawmakers failed to notice the last-minute exemption that paved the way for bailed-out companies like AIG to pay out substantial bonuses. In response, the House scrambled last week to clean up the mess by rushing through yet another bill—a tax on AIG bonuses. That bill was a mere 11 hours old before it reached the floor to be debated and then swiftly approved.

And this pattern extends well beyond the current administration. The bank bailout received all of 29 hours of consideration, while the rescue of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac was available for review for only 19 hours. This is precisely how bills can become, to borrow a phrase, too big to fail—and too fast to stop.

The Sunlight Foundation is calling on Congress to grant the American people three days—72 hours—to read a nonemergency bill online before debate begins. We wholeheartedly agree. And yes, lawmakers: you, too, deserve three full days to review the legislation before taking a stand.

As for President Obama's pledge of a five-day public review once a bill leaves Capitol Hill bound for his desk, it would be commendable if he honored that commitment going forward.

*The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of Campbell Brown.*

Then consider Congress and the Stimulus Bill. How quickly could you plow through it? The nonpartisan Sunlight Foundation reports that legislators were given a mere 13 hours to absorb 1,100 pages of content carrying a price tag of $787 billion for American taxpayers. Do the math and that works out to under 90 seconds per page—and forget about pausing to use the restroom.

It's hardly surprising, then, that many members of Congress apparently overlooked the eleventh-hour provision that opened the door for companies receiving bailouts, such as AIG, to hand out enormous bonuses. In response, the House scrambled last week to fix the situation by fast-tracking yet another measure—a tax targeting those AIG bonuses. That legislation was a mere 11 hours old when it reached the floor for debate and was promptly passed.

This pattern stretches back even before Obama assumed the presidency. Lawmakers had just 29 hours with the bank bailout, while the Fannie and Freddie rescue was accessible for only 19 hours. This is precisely how legislation can become—to steal a familiar expression—too big to fail, and too rushed to halt.

The Sunlight Foundation is urging Congress to grant Americans a full three days, or 72 hours, to examine nonemergency legislation online before any debate kicks off. We wholeheartedly support this idea. And yes, lawmakers, that same three-day window applies to you as well—read the bill before you commit to a position.

Regarding Obama's vow to allow five days of public examination once a bill departs Capitol Hill and reaches his desk, it would be commendable for him to honor that commitment moving forward.

The views presented in this commentary belong exclusively to Campbell Brown.

# Broken Promises on Government Transparency

Both the White House and Congress have failed to uphold the transparency standards that President Obama promised during his campaign. Despite pledges to make government more open and accountable, the actual practices of both the executive and legislative branches have fallen short of these commitments, leaving citizens with little opportunity to scrutinize the legislation being enacted on their behalf.

One of the earliest breaches of these promises came when President Obama signed the Lilly Ledbetter Bill barely a week after taking office. In doing so, he broke his own commitment to allow five days of public review before signing legislation into law. This early departure from a signature campaign pledge set a troubling precedent for the administration's approach to transparency.

The problem became even more pronounced with the passage of the Stimulus Bill. Lawmakers were given only 13 hours to read the 1,100-page document—amounting to less than a minute and a half per page for legislation that would cost taxpayers $787 billion. Such a compressed timeline made meaningful review virtually impossible, effectively asking legislators to vote on a massive spending package they could not have realistically read in full.

The consequences of this rushed process were not merely theoretical. In their haste, legislators missed a last-minute exemption buried in the bill that allowed bailed-out companies like AIG to pay large bonuses. Had lawmakers been afforded adequate time to examine the legislation, this controversial provision might have been caught and addressed before the bill became law.

Unfortunately, this pattern of hastily reviewed legislation is not unique to the current administration. Similar failures have characterized other major financial measures in recent years. The bank bailout received only 29 hours of review, while the Fannie and Freddie rescue was afforded just 19 hours. Taken together, these examples reveal a systemic problem in Washington—one in which enormous, consequential decisions are made without giving lawmakers or the public a fair chance to understand what is being passed.

# The Broken Promise of Transparency: When Rushed Legislation Fails the American People

During his presidential campaign, Barack Obama made a specific and meaningful commitment to the American people regarding government transparency. He pledged that nonemergency legislation would be posted publicly for a full five days before he signed it into law, giving citizens and their representatives adequate time to review, understand, and respond to the measures being enacted. This promise reflected a broader vision of open governance—one in which the legislative process would not happen behind closed doors or under cover of artificial urgency, but rather in full view of the public it was meant to serve.

Unfortunately, both the White House and Congress have repeatedly failed to honor this commitment. Rather than allowing time for thoughtful deliberation, lawmakers have often rushed major bills through the legislative process at breakneck speed. The Stimulus Bill stands as a particularly striking example of this failure. This sweeping piece of legislation spanned approximately 1,100 pages, yet members of Congress were given only thirteen hours to read it before casting their votes. By any reasonable standard, this timeframe made genuine review impossible. No legislator, however diligent, could realistically absorb and evaluate the full contents of such a massive and complex document in so brief a window.

The consequences of this rushed approach quickly became apparent. When legislation is passed without adequate scrutiny, important provisions can slip through unnoticed—and that is precisely what happened. Buried within the Stimulus Bill was a clause that permitted companies receiving taxpayer-funded bailouts, including the insurance giant AIG, to continue paying out substantial bonuses to their executives. This provision sparked widespread public outrage once it came to light, as ordinary Americans questioned why struggling taxpayers should subsidize lavish compensation for the very institutions whose failures had contributed to the economic crisis.

This episode illustrates a broader and troubling truth: when legislation is passed hastily, without the transparency and review time that responsible governance demands, the results can be costly and difficult to reverse. The failure to honor the five-day review pledge was not merely a broken campaign promise—it had real financial implications for taxpayers who bore the burden of provisions that might have been challenged or removed under proper scrutiny. Ultimately, this experience underscores the vital importance of transparency and deliberation in the legislative process, reminding us that the speed at which a bill passes should never come at the expense of the public's right to know what their government is doing in their name.

# The Editor's Role in Shaping a Story

Every great publication relies on more than just talented writers—it depends on the sharp instincts of a skilled editor. The editor serves as the guardian of clarity, ensuring that each piece of writing is polished, accurate, and engaging before it reaches the public.

Consider the working relationship between a seasoned editor named Brown and an ambitious reporter named Campbell. When Campbell submitted her first major feature, it was passionate but rough around the edges. Brown, with years of experience behind him, sat down with her to review the draft line by line.

"Your reporting is solid," Brown explained, "but the structure needs work. A reader should never feel lost." Campbell listened carefully, taking notes as her editor pointed out where the argument wandered and where the strongest details had been buried too deep in the text.

Over the following weeks, the collaboration between Campbell and Brown grew into a productive partnership. He challenged her to dig deeper into her sources, while she brought fresh energy and new ideas to the newsroom. The editor's guidance did not stifle her voice—instead, it sharpened it.

By the time Campbell's story was published, it had transformed from a promising draft into a compelling piece of journalism. Brown had done what every good editor does: he helped a talented writer produce her very best work, all while remaining largely invisible to the final reader.

This is the quiet power of editing. Behind nearly every memorable article stands an editor like Brown, dedicated to excellence and committed to helping writers like Campbell tell stories that truly matter.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN commentary segment for "Campbell Brown: No Bias, No Bull" criticizing the Obama White House and Congress for failing to give the public enough time to read legislation before it's passed.
counterfactuals.output:
# No Bias, No Bull

## Campbell Brown Commentary

---

Tonight, I want to talk about a promise. A promise made by candidate Barack Obama, who told the American people that his would be the most transparent administration in history.

He pledged that when a bill landed on his desk, the public would have five days to read it online before he signed it. Five days. That was the promise.

So let me ask a simple question: What happened to it?

Because here's what we're seeing instead. Massive bills—hundreds, sometimes over a thousand pages long—rushed through Congress at breakneck speed. Legislation that will affect every American, spending money we don't have, voted on before anyone has actually read the whole thing.

I'm not talking about Democrats or Republicans here. This is a bipartisan disease. Both parties do it when it's convenient, and both parties complain about it when they're out of power. The stimulus bill, the various spending packages—lawmakers admitted, out loud, that they hadn't read them before voting yes.

Think about that. The people we elected, the people spending your tax dollars, casting votes on bills they never read. And the White House, which promised sunlight, signing them without giving you—the public—the time to weigh in.

Here's the thing. When you rush something this big, this expensive, this consequential, you're not governing. You're gambling. You're betting that nobody will notice what's buried on page 800. And too often, the special interests and the lobbyists—they've read it. They know exactly what's in there. It's just the American people who are left in the dark.

Transparency isn't a slogan you trot out during a campaign and forget about once you're in office. It's a discipline. It means slowing down. It means posting the bill, letting the public read it, letting the press dig into it, letting the sunlight in—even when it's inconvenient. *Especially* when it's inconvenient.

So tonight, my message to the White House and to Congress is simple: Keep your promise. Give us the five days. Give us the time to read what you're passing in our name.

No bias, no bull. Just a promise worth keeping.

I'm Campbell Brown.

---

*This is a fictional commentary written in the style of the program, which aired on CNN from 2008 to 2010.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an opinion piece arguing that Congress should give Americans 72 hours to read nonemergency bills online before debate, citing examples like the Stimulus Bill, the AIG bonus tax, and the bank bailout.
counterfactuals.output:
# Give Us 72 Hours: Congress Should Let Americans Read Bills Before They Become Law

There is something deeply wrong with how Washington passes the laws that govern our lives. Bills spanning hundreds—sometimes thousands—of pages routinely land on lawmakers' desks mere hours before a vote. If members of Congress themselves cannot read the legislation they're voting on, what chance do ordinary Americans have of understanding what their government is doing in their name?

It's time for a simple, common-sense reform: Congress should be required to post the full text of any nonemergency bill online for at least 72 hours before debate begins. Three days. That's all we're asking.

## A Pattern of Rushed Legislation

Consider the recent record.

The **economic stimulus bill** of 2009—a package exceeding $800 billion and running more than 1,000 pages—was posted in its final form late one Thursday night and passed the next day. Lawmakers had roughly 13 hours to digest one of the largest spending bills in American history. Not a single member could honestly claim to have read it, let alone weighed its long-term consequences for taxpayers and future generations.

The **bank bailout**—the Troubled Asset Relief Program—authorized $700 billion in a matter of days amid an atmosphere of crisis and pressure. Americans watched their representatives commit staggering sums with little public scrutiny and no meaningful opportunity for citizens to weigh in before the deal was done.

Then came the **AIG bonus tax**. When public outrage erupted over bonuses paid to executives at a bailed-out company, the House rushed through a 90 percent tax targeting those payments within days. Whatever one thinks of the bonuses, hastily written tax law crafted in the heat of anger is precisely the kind of legislation most likely to produce constitutional problems and unintended consequences. Cooler heads and a few days of sunlight might have produced a more defensible response.

## Why 72 Hours Matters

Critics will say government must sometimes act fast. True—which is why this rule would apply only to *nonemergency* legislation. Genuine emergencies could be handled through a transparent waiver, on the record, so voters know exactly who chose to bypass the process and why.

But most bills are not emergencies. Most are the product of months of committee work, negotiation, and drafting. There is no legitimate reason a finished bill cannot sit in public view for three days before a vote.

The benefits are considerable:

- **Accountability.** When citizens, journalists, and watchdog groups can read a bill, they can flag hidden provisions, special-interest carve-outs, and last-minute additions before they become law.
- **Deliberation.** A brief cooling-off period discourages the kind of panic-driven lawmaking that produces regret. Good policy rarely suffers from an extra 72 hours of thought.
- **Trust.** Public confidence in government is corroded by the sense that deals are cut behind closed doors and rammed through before anyone can object. Transparency is an antidote.

## Sunlight Is Not a Partisan Value

This is not a proposal that favors one party over another. Both parties have used rushed procedures when in power, and both have complained loudly when out of it. A 72-hour rule would apply equally to everyone, in every session, regardless of who holds the majority.

Technology has removed every excuse. Posting a bill online costs almost nothing and takes minutes. The only real obstacle is the preference of some in power for speed over scrutiny—and that is precisely the instinct a waiting period is meant to check.

## A Modest Reform With Outsized Rewards

Seventy-two hours will not fix everything wrong with Congress. It will not end special-interest influence or guarantee wise legislation. But it will restore a basic principle that ought to be beyond dispute in a self-governing republic: that the people, and the representatives who serve them, deserve the chance to know what they are being asked to accept.

The laws Congress passes belong to all of us. The least our lawmakers can do is let us read them first.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output:
# Cutting Through the Bull: The Transparency Promise

Let's talk tonight about a promise—one made not once, not twice, but repeatedly, with hand-on-heart sincerity, to the American people.

The promise was simple: transparency. We were told that legislation—the big bills, the ones that reshape how you live, what you pay, what your government does with your money—would be posted online for the public to read. Five days. That was the pledge. Five days for you, the citizen, and yes, for the reporters and watchdogs whose job it is to tell you what's actually in these things, to read them before a single vote was cast.

Sounds reasonable, doesn't it? A few days to read what our representatives are about to sign into law in your name.

So here's where I cut through the bull.

That promise has been broken. Repeatedly. By both parties, I might add—because this isn't about left or right tonight. It's about the gap between what politicians say and what they do.

Bills hundreds—sometimes thousands—of pages long get dropped in the dead of night and voted on before the ink is dry. Before anyone, and I mean anyone, could have possibly read them. Lawmakers themselves admit—admit, on camera—that they haven't read the bills they're voting on. Think about that. The people writing your laws don't have time to read them, and they certainly didn't give you the time they promised.

And when we ask why? We get the excuses. It's urgent. It's an emergency. There's no time. The other side is playing politics.

Here's the thing. There's always an emergency. There's always a reason the rules everyone agreed to don't apply this particular time. And when the rule is broken every single time it becomes inconvenient—it was never really a rule at all. It was a talking point.

Transparency isn't transparency if you only offer it when it costs you nothing.

So to the leaders of both parties who looked into the camera and made this promise: we remember. We wrote it down. And a promise you break the moment it's inconvenient isn't a principle.

It's a bull.

And that's cutting through it. We'll be right back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a 500-word editorial calling out President Obama for breaking his campaign promise to allow five days of public comment on nonemergency bills, using the Lilly Ledbetter Act as an example.
counterfactuals.output:
# A Broken Promise on Transparency

When Barack Obama campaigned for the presidency, he made a specific pledge that resonated with Americans hungry for open government: he promised to post nonemergency legislation online for five days of public comment before signing it into law. This commitment, part of his broader "Sunlight Before Signing" initiative, was meant to restore public trust and give citizens a meaningful voice in the legislative process. Yet within days of taking office, that promise was already broken.

The Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act stands as a glaring early example. On January 29, 2009, President Obama signed this legislation into law with great fanfare, making it the first major bill of his presidency. Whatever one's views on the merits of the law itself, the manner of its signing directly contradicted his campaign rhetoric. The bill was signed almost immediately after passing Congress, denying the American public the five-day window Obama had explicitly promised.

This matters not because the Ledbetter Act was necessarily bad policy, but because of what the broken promise reveals about the gap between campaign rhetoric and governing reality. Transparency pledges are easy to make on the campaign trail and apparently just as easy to abandon once in office. If the very first significant bill couldn't wait five days, what does that say about the sincerity of the original commitment?

Defenders might argue that the five-day rule was aspirational, or that certain bills warranted expedited treatment. But the Ledbetter Act was hardly an emergency measure requiring instant enactment. The pay discrimination issues it addressed had persisted for years; a five-day comment period would not have caused any meaningful harm. The rush to sign it appears driven more by the desire for a symbolic early victory than by any genuine urgency.

The pattern would continue throughout the administration. Analysis by watchdog groups found that the five-day pledge was honored inconsistently at best, with numerous bills signed well before the promised waiting period elapsed. What was billed as a firm commitment became, in practice, a suggestion honored in the breach.

This episode offers a lesson that transcends partisan lines. Voters across the political spectrum should hold politicians accountable for the specific promises they make, particularly promises about the process of governing itself. Process commitments—how decisions get made, how transparent the government will be—deserve special scrutiny because they shape the very legitimacy of democratic government.

President Obama entered office promising to be different, to run the most transparent administration in history. The immediate abandonment of the five-day comment rule suggests those promises deserved more skepticism than they received. Americans were told they would have a window to review and respond to legislation before it became law. That window was slammed shut almost immediately.

Accountability requires that we remember such promises and measure leaders against them. The Lilly Ledbetter Act may have been signed with celebration, but it also signed away an early opportunity for the administration to prove its commitment to the transparency it so loudly championed.

# When Speed Trumps Scrutiny: Congress and the Vanishing Reading Window

*A Commentary*

There's an old expectation, perhaps a naive one, that the people writing our laws have actually read them. Yet time and again, some of the most consequential legislation in modern American history has landed on lawmakers' desks with barely enough time to skim the table of contents.

Consider two defining moments of the financial crisis era. The 2008 Emergency Economic Stabilization Act—the $700 billion bank bailout—and the 2009 American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, the roughly $787 billion stimulus package, were each rushed to votes with remarkably little time for review. According to analysis circulated by the Sunlight Foundation, a government transparency group, lawmakers had only a handful of hours with the final text before casting votes that would reshape the economy for a generation. The stimulus bill, more than a thousand pages long, was reportedly posted late at night and voted on the following day—leaving legislators and the public little practical opportunity to digest what they were approving.

The math is unforgiving. No human being can meaningfully absorb a thousand pages of dense legislative language, cross-referenced statutes, and buried appropriations in a single overnight window. When bills of this magnitude move that fast, "reading the bill" becomes a fiction, and lawmakers are effectively voting on trust—trusting leadership, trusting staff summaries, trusting that nothing objectionable was slipped into the fine print.

Defenders of speed have a legitimate argument: crises don't wait. In the autumn of 2008, credit markets were seizing, and every day of delay carried real economic risk. Sometimes governing means acting before you have the luxury of a leisurely review. Emergencies are, by definition, urgent.

But urgency is also the most convenient cover for avoiding accountability. The same procedural rush that lets Congress respond to a genuine crisis can bury pork, protect special interests, and shield unpopular provisions from public debate. A democracy depends not just on outcomes but on process—on citizens being able to see what their representatives are doing before it becomes law. Transparency advocates have long pushed for mandatory waiting periods, such as a 72-hour public posting requirement, precisely to restore that basic accountability without paralyzing government in a true emergency.

The lesson from the bailout and stimulus votes isn't that Congress should never move quickly. It's that "we didn't have time to read it" should be an admission of failure, not a routine feature of how Washington operates. When speed becomes the norm rather than the exception, the losers are the citizens who are governed by laws no one fully understood.

---

*The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.*
